items.excerpt: 06 November 2026• Update: 06 November 2026 BERLIN Here’s a rundown of all the news you need to start your Friday, including US President Donald Trump warning that Iran could face further destruction, Türkiye’s parliament approving a trilateral defense pact with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, and Israel's president to announce Sunday who will be tasked with forming government. US President Donald Trump said he may have to “destroy the rest” of Iran and that “you’ll know soon enough.” “Now we’ll make a decision: Do we want to go further and just certify it, by certifying it meaning it will never happen again?” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. “I would rather not destroy the rest of the country, if possible, but maybe I’ll have to. And you’ll know soon enough,” he said. Trump also dismissed speculation that he is considering replacing Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, stating that “he’s doing a very good job.” - Turkish parliament approves Mecca joint defense pact with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia The Turkish parliament approved a bill ratifying the Mecca Agreement on Joint Defense between Türkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, clearing the way for the trilateral security pact to take effect. Lawmakers endorsed the measure by 279 votes to 119, with 398 of the chamber’s 592 members taking part in the ballot. During the debate, ruling Justice and Development (AK) Party lawmaker Ziya Altunyaldiz stressed that the agreement aims to expand security cooperation in the region. He emphasized that it contains no approach against any third country and that its main goal is to prevent conflicts rather than escalate them. - Israel's president to announce Sunday who will be tasked with forming government Israel’s president said he will announce Sunday which lawmaker will be tasked with forming the next government following consultations with political parties following last month’s elections. In a Thursday video message reported by Israeli news outlet Ynet, Isaac Herzog said parties representing 67 members of the 120-seat Knesset recommended Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot, while parties holding 46 seats backed current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, leader of the Likud party. “The results of the consultations may appear clear,” Herzog said, but added that the ability to form a government remains uncertain due to mutual objections between and within political blocs. He said he would hold further individual talks with party leaders to assess their prospects of forming a coalition. Herzog stressed that he would make every effort to facilitate the formation of a stable government.

items.excerpt: Stephen Wolfe - 10 Things News Nov 06, 2026 1. AI Sell-Off Wipes $2.5 Trillion From Nasdaq (Markets) 2. Republican Defeat Opens Up The 2028 Presidential Race (US) 3. Iran And US Review Nuclear Proposals Amid War Threat (Diplomacy) 4. Saudi Arabia Faces Costly Choices Over Houthi Threat (Middle East) 5. Israel’s Election Leaves Netanyahu’s Future Uncertain (Politics) 6. France Sees Mass Protests Over Wages And Living Costs (Europe) 7. Bomb Hoaxes Disrupt Dozens Of Flights Across Europe (Europe) 8. Sudan And Ethiopia Expel Diplomats As Tensions Rise (Africa) 9. Newsom Commutes All 548 California Death Sentences (US) 10. Climate Threats Put 90 Million Displaced People At Risk (Climate) Global technology shares plunged after Democratic victories in the US midterm elections raised concerns about restrictions on artificial intelligence infrastructure. The Nasdaq Composite fell more than 5.5% on Thursday, wiping an estimated $2.5 trillion from its market value and entering correction territory. Nvidia lost more than 9%, while semiconductor stocks suffered even steeper declines. Democrats won control of both houses of Congress after campaigns that included opposition to rapid data centre expansion. Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has called for a moratorium on new approvals. Investors were already questioning whether enormous spending on AI infrastructure would generate expected returns, while tighter approvals could delay projects and increase costs. The sell-off spread into Asian markets on Friday. Japan’s Nikkei fell 6% in early trading, South Korea’s Kospi dropped more than 8.5%, triggering a trading halt and Taiwan’s Taiex lost over 8.3%. The S&P 500 also fell 4.4%. ###### Sources: BBC, Wall Street Journal Republicans’ sweeping midterm defeat has thrown the party’s 2028 presidential succession into uncertainty, with Vice President JD Vance distancing himself from President Donald Trump’s Iran war and potential rivals positioning themselves for a contest. Vance blamed the war for the losses, calling for an end to the conflict, greater attention to affordability and a reassessment of US relations with Israel. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis described the result as an “extinction-level event” for Republicans, while Senator Ted Cruz criticised the war’s duration and the party’s failure to address voters’ economic concerns. Vance remains the nomination front-runner, supported by influential donors and conservative organisations but Trump’s endorsement has not materialised. Meanwhile, Democrats’ capture of both congressional chambers gives them greater scope to challenge the administration’s war policy through funding restrictions and investigations. The defeat has intensified debate over the party’s direction beyond Trump. Iran and the United States are reviewing nuclear proposals through Qatari mediation, signalling renewed diplomatic engagement as both sides weigh the risk of further military escalation. A senior Iranian official said Tehran had submitted a proposal to Washington, while other officials described discussions of concrete terms for Iran’s nuclear programme. Iran’s Supreme National Security Council chief Mohsen Rezaei publicly maintained that negotiations and reopening the Strait of Hormuz depend on Washington meeting seven demands, including sanctions relief and the release of frozen assets. Privately, however, officials said he had shown greater willingness to discuss nuclear issues. US Vice President JD Vance has supported the mediation effort, while President Donald Trump has retained the option of renewed strikes. Iran’s highly enriched uranium stockpile remains a central obstacle, with Tehran opposing its removal from the country. The diplomatic activity follows weeks of confrontation and warnings of wider regional retaliation. Saudi Arabia faces mounting military and diplomatic difficulties as Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis intensify attacks on its oil facilities and airports while advancing towards Aden, the seat of Yemen’s internationally recognised government. The militants reportedly demanded $51 billion and recognition as Yemen’s rulers in return for ending hostilities, although Saudi Deputy Minister Rayed Krimly denied that any financial demand had been made. The Houthis have moved within roughly 50 miles of Aden, while repeated strikes on Saudi infrastructure have disrupted travel and damaged energy facilities. Saudi airstrikes have failed to halt their advance, and deploying ground forces risks heavy casualties. Riyadh’s options are further constrained by limited allied support. The United Arab Emirates has withdrawn from the campaign, while Pakistan and Egypt have ruled out offensive operations. Any settlement involving payments could also establish a precedent for further demands, leaving Saudi Arabia facing ... California Governor Gavin Newsom has commuted the death sentences of all 548 prisoners on the state’s death row to life imprisonment without parole, in the largest mass commutation of its kind in modern US history. The decision affects roughly a quarter of death sentences nationwide, although some cases require approval from California’s Supreme Court. Newsom called capital punishment morally objectionable and said its application was unfair. California has not carried out an execution for 20 years, and the governor imposed a moratorium in 2019. His latest decision does not abolish the death penalty, which remains part of state law. The move has divided victims’ families and is expected to face legal challenges. Former Sacramento district attorney Anne Marie Schubert argues that cases must be reviewed individually, while other legal experts say collective consideration may be possible. Newsom acknowledged that the commutations could revive painful memories for victims’ relatives. Nearly 90 million forcibly displaced people, about three-quarters of the global total, live in countries highly exposed to drought, flooding and extreme heat, the UN refugee agency said ahead of COP31 in Turkey. The agency warned that climate hazards are compounding the difficulties facing people displaced by conflict and persecution.

items.title: US inflation too high; essential to get back to 2%: Fed’s Williams By Reuters
items.excerpt: Published Nov 06, 2026, 05:31 AM Updated Nov 06, 2026, 05:36 AM ... FRANKFURT, Nov 6 (Reuters) - US economic growth has remained resilient and the labour market is remarkably stable despite successive shocks, but inflation is too high and must be brought back to 2%, New York Federal Reserve President John Williams said on Friday. Inflation has soared across the world, mostly as the US war on Iran has pushed energy prices higher but also because soaring investment in AI has pushed up costs for some IT-related products and services. "Inflation is absolutely too high. It’s been too high for too long," Williams told a European Central Bank conference in Frankfurt. "It’s absolutely essential that we bring inflation back to our 2% target in a timely manner and a sustained basis." But Williams also argued that the Fed’s key focus should be on where inflation is heading and making sure that current shocks do not translate into broader or more persistent inflation. "Fortunately, we’re not seeing that happen so far in terms of inflation expectations, which remain well anchored," Williams said. "We’re seeing wage growth (that is), I think, consistent with our 2% goal." While Williams did not discuss what the Fed’s next policy move should be, he said the bank’s last policy statement had correctly concluded that it was appropriate for the Fed to collect more information to determine what the appropriate stance of policy is. Financial markets see a more than 50% chance of a rate hike by the Fed in December while a move by March is fully priced in.

items.title: Democrat win gives markets a reason to rethink path of interest rates
items.excerpt: - Democrats’ electoral success initially lifted hopes that Trump will seek a deal to end the Iran war, easing oil prices and inflation pressures. - However, a peace deal would not erase existing energy pressures overnight, and analysts say any resolution to conflict is far from guaranteed. - Fiscal policy and a potential slowdown in the AI buildout under the new Congress will shape the U.S. growth outlook, with one analyst warning tighter spending and slower investment could risk a mid-cycle economic slowdown in 2027 — meaning the Fed should act with caution on rate hikes. ... The high level of U.S. fiscal stimulus and whether it is about to change is the "million dollar question" right now, James Sullivan, managing director and head of Asia Pacific equity research at J.P. Morgan, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia." "The reasons why you're seeing inflation running high is a combination of a range of factors, from the war in Iran, to tariffs, to significant tightness in particular areas of the energy complex," he said. "But it's also important to recognize the U.S. government has continued to spend at very high levels, into an economic expansion with low unemployment, and that's driving very specific macroeconomic implications. If that changes, you potentially take the pressure off the rate environment in a way that gives the Fed significantly more forward flexibility." Daniel Clifton, head of policy research at Baird Strategas, said the impact on the data center buildout in the U.S. was another big factor to watch. "In 2025, we had major fiscal headwinds, and it really didn't matter because we had such a big capex boom in the AI build-out last year. This year was driven a lot by stimulus," he told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe." "If you have an environment where you have tighter fiscal policy — the Fed is raising rates right now — and you have a slowdown in the AI capex build out, you're probably going to reach a policy mistake at some point in mid-2027," he said. "That's what happened in 2000 during the Y2K tech boom, the Fed was raising rates, we had higher oil prices, and they just went too far, and eventually it had a recession. Our forecast is not for a recession in the United States. Our forecast is that we'll have a mid-cycle slowdown in 2027."

items.title: Markets fret over growth and inflation despite easing oil prices By Reuters
items.excerpt: LONDON, Nov 6 (Reuters) - Uncertainty over the growth outlook and expectations that inflation will remain elevated next year are weighing on global markets, even as hopes of a de-escalation in the Iran war have eased oil prices. Government borrowing costs have risen sharply this year, the tech-led Nasdaq racked up on Thursday its biggest one-day drop since April 2025’s Liberation Day rout and European economic data has softened. The combination is fuelling concern that inflation could stay high even as growth slows, although the Democratic victory in US midterm elections has raised hopes for an eventual end to the Iran war. OIL STILL HIGH Oil has fallen 15% this week to just below $100 a barrel. But analysts warn that any resolution to the Iran war remains uncertain, leaving scope for prices to rise again. Oil is still up 64% this year, while natural gas remains nearly three times its level at the start of 2026. That backdrop is keeping near-term inflation expectations elevated and reinforcing concerns that price pressures could persist as growth slows, forcing central banks to raise interest rates further. The University of Michigan’s measure of one-year US inflation expectations edged up to 4.7% in October from 4.6% in September and ​3.4% in February. Market measures of long-term inflation expectations remain above 2% in the euro zone and the US, and above 3% in Britain. Higher energy costs add to inflation while also weighing on growth by increasing transport, manufacturing and household expenses. AllianceBernstein chief investment strategist Inigo Fraser Jenkins said the geopolitical tensions and supply disruptions driving inflationary pressures would persist beyond the US midterms. "Today it’s oil, but next time it could be cobalt, lithium or something else, and we need to get used to that," he said. "It will manifest itself in the form of higher inflation and greater volatility." FOOD PRICES BITE Food prices, driven higher by extreme weather, shipping disruptions and elevated energy costs, remain a key inflation concern. The United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization’s Food Price Index is at its highest level in nearly four years. Costs could rise further, with major consumer goods and food companies warning of price increases to offset higher expenses, while Britain’s leading retail trade body has flagged similar concerns. Food inflation can also fuel broader economic pressures, said Hank Calenti, global markets strategist at SMBC. "Food inflation makes people start to think that ’there’s really inflation here and it’s going to stay high and I need to get a better job or my employer needs to pay me more’," he said. "So, those second-round effects come in." ... RJ Gallo, chief investment officer for global fixed income at Federated Hermes, cautioned against overusing the term stagflation, which describes a combination of high inflation, weak growth and elevated unemployment. He noted that the US economy continues to grow at a solid pace and that unemployment, at 4.2%, remains low by historical standards, adding that "inflation continues to be the Fed’s primary concern".

items.title: White House denies Hegseth, Rubio will leave jobs amid Republican election fallout
items.excerpt: The White House has denied rumours that Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio might leave their jobs in a post-election shakeup of the Trump administration. US media have reported there are calls to replace Hegseth - in particular over his handling of the Iran war, which is being blamed for heavy Republican election losses. One outgoing congressional Republican has threatened to force an impeachment vote against Hegseth as early as next week. The defence secretary posted a video statement defending his record and denouncing the effort. "You see, they attack me. They attack us because we are effective," he said. "It's not going to work. We will not back down." ## Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war Meanwhile, Rubio is denying reports he is considering leaving his post ahead of a 2028 presidential run. Working for Trump until the end of his term has "always been my plan," Rubio told The New York Times in an interview. "I love the work I'm doing," Rubio said. "And plus I always laugh when they say he's going to leave his job. I go, 'Which one?'" The White House and US State Department also shut down reports that Rubio might be leaving after this week's midterm losses, with both calling it "fake news". The defence secretary, though, faces a more uncertain political future. Trump and Vice-President JD Vance have both blamed the Iran war for Republican losses that allowed Democrats full control of the US House of Representatives and the Senate. In a telephone interview with ABC News, Trump said that he had received "calls about" Hegseth, but added that he had "every intention" of keeping him. Later on Thursday, he told reporters at the White House that "Pete Hegseth has done a fantastic job", and went on to list what he sees are some of his achievements, including the arrest of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro in January and the Iran war, now into its ninth month. ... Meanwhile, Republican Representative Thomas Massie, a frequent critic of Trump, has said he will push ahead with plans to push for Hegseth's impeachment.

items.excerpt: Here's a summary of today's key moments: - Donald Trump has signed his first official action since the Republicans suffered a landslide defeat - Trump has thrown his support behind Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has been facing criticism in the wake of the Republican midterm election results. - The US president has also suggested he may seek to expand his administration's war in Iran. - Meanwhile, Democrats are continuing to notch up wins in the US House of Representatives, extending their majority in the chamber. - Two US Senate seats remain in doubt, with counting continuing in Alaska and Mississippi. ... ### Mississippi Senate race could be headed for a legal battle By Audrey Courty This is one of the Senate races we've been watching closely and the fight over the final result is getting more complicated. Democrat Scott Colom is narrowly leading Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi, with 96% of the votes counted. Scott Colom is leading by a razor-thin margin. (AP Photo: Mississippi Today) Colom is ahead by about 1,800 votes, with reportedly thousands of provisional ballots still outstanding. In Mississippi, these are known as "affidavit ballots" and they include votes cast by people who had issues with their identification or weren't listed on the electoral roll at their polling place. Mississippi Today reports the National Republican Senatorial Committee, which supports Hyde-Smith, has asked election officials in all 82 counties to preserve these ballots in case they're needed in future legal proceedings. According to local broadcaster WLOX, Colom's campaign has pushed back, arguing the request is unlawful and could compromise voters' privacy. Mississippi has no automatic recount process, meaning a recount would need to be ordered by a court. For now, no lawsuit has been filed yet, but both sides appear to be preparing for a possible legal dispute over the final count.

items.title: Lil Baby & JENNIE Lead Best New Music: Friday Music Guide
items.excerpt: 11/6/2026 # Lil Baby, JENNIE, Dove Cameron, XG, Boys Noize & More: New Music Friday Guide Check out the must-hear releases of the week. ... Billboard’s Friday Music Guide serves as a handy guide to New Music Friday’s most essential releases each week — the key music that everyone will be talking about today, and that will be dominating playlists this weekend and beyond. This week, Lil Baby is back with his anticipated fifth album; JENNIE drops a new single for the animated Netflix film STEPS; Dove Cameron releases her long-awaited debut album; and Boys Noize returns with his first solo studio album in five years.… plus much more. Check out all of this week’s picks below: Lil Baby, Fresh After scoring his third consecutive Billboard 200 No. 1 album with WHAM last year, Lil Baby is gunning for his fourth with Fresh. The new set arrives with a title inspired by his recent hit single “Dead Fresh,” an infectious, Pharrell-produced joint that soared to No. 18 on the Billboard Hot 100 and topped Rhythmic Airplay. Stacked with guest appearances by frequent collaborators Future, Young Thug and Rylo Rodriguez, Fresh finds Baby delivering 17 new songs that reassert his position as one of the most gifted mainstream MCs to blow up this decade. — KYLE DENIS JENNIE, “Someone To Hold” The inviting disco-colored intro of “Someone To Hold” neither sounds like a typical song for JENNIE nor a Disney princess — and that’s what makes it magic. The colorful pop song shows a new side of JENNIE’s artistry that leans more playful and vibrant than anything on her solo debut full-length, while also matching the fresh take of the movie it’s from — as the upcoming musical comedy Steps reimagines Cinderella from the perspective of the stepsisters. — L.H. Dove Cameron, Final Girl Despite launching her career over a decade ago in Disney TV and film franchises — also lending her voice to both — Final Girl is Dove Cameron’s debut full-length. At long last. The dramatic and soaring album delivers a range of tempos and emotions, from softer songs like pop ballad “Silver Screen Baby” and the raw “Immortalized” to uptempo dance-pop single “When In Rome” and the haunting and heavy “Skin On Bone.” It’s an album that was well worth the wait, and offers so much possibility and intrigue as to what sounds and styles Cameron will want to explore next. — L.H. Kings Of Leon, “Rose” Veteran rock band Kings Of Leon has released its 10th album, O My Beloved — and the first the band has ever self-produced. That decision paid off, as the gorgeous album marries thoughtful and melodic production with deeply personal storytelling about the member’s families and upbringings. Described in a press release as a “love letter” to the road that brought the band to this point, it feels just as much a love letter to the fans who have walked that road with them for more than two decades. — L.H. XG, “Depends” Since debuting in 2022, Japanese girl group XG have kept busy — especially this year. Since releasing its first full-length in January, titled THE CORE – 核, the group has embarked on its second world tour and has now, amidst that outing, released more new music with “Depends.” The electro-pop track showcases the members vocal strengths, from hard-hitting raps to syrupy, soaring high notes — all of which are united ... Slayyyter, “Hey Boyyy” In just one month, on Dec. 4, Slayyyter will unveil the counterpart to this year’s acclaimed WOR$T GIRL IN AMERICA album. Aptly titled wor$t man in america, the new album will contrast the perspectives she shared and ideas she explored on its predecessor. Frenetic new single “Hey Boyyy” delivers on Slayyyter’s signature sound thought is a bit softer in its lyrics, striking a balance only she can between a chaotic nature with good intentions. ... Boys Noize, 7LLVSION ... And now the producer returns to himself with 7LLVSION, his first solo studio album in five years. ... Jack Harlow, Sweet Action II

Salman, who headlines the Apoorva Lakhia-directed movie, based on the 2020 Galwan Valley clash between Indian and Chinese troops, shared the release date at the film's promotional event here. Asked about the delay in the film's release, Salman said the team wanted to ensure that the visual effects were up to the mark. Nov 06, 2026, 3:56 pm IST Ramayana: Part One, the grand retelling of the Hindu mythological epic, made a blockbuster start at the worldwide box office, collection Rs 155 crore gross on its opening day, the makers said on Friday. Directed by Nitesh Tiwari, the film released worldwide on November 5, featuring Ranbir Kapoor as Lord Rama, Sai Pallavi as Sita, Yash as Ravana and Ravi Dubey as Lakshmana. In a press note, the makers said that the movie has registered the highest pre-Diwali opening in the history of Indian cinema. "Making a remarkable start at the global box office, 'Ramayana' has collected a staggering Rs 155 crore worldwide gross on its opening day, emerging as the highest Day 1 Pre-Diwali opener in the history of Indian cinema," the note read. The lineup also features Karol G, Bizarrap, Baby Ranks, Bad Gyal, Miguel Colón, Divino, DJ Premier, Grupo Niche, Jay Wheeler, Lil Supa, Luis Enrique, Nathy Peluso and Ángel "Cucco" Pena. Nov 06, 2026, 1:11 pm IST ... ## Ramayana Box Office Collection Day 1 As per Sacnilk, Ramayana opened at Rs. 64.85 crore net across all languages in India, while its first-day gross collection stood at Rs. 77.50 crore. The film was expected to make a bigger impact at the box office, with trade expectations suggesting that its opening-day net earnings could cross the Rs. 80 crore mark. However, the actual figures fell short of that target. Released in five languages — Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam and Kannada — the film recorded its highest collection from the Hindi version. It earned Rs. 47.50 crore net in Hindi alone. The Kannada version came second with Rs. 7.25 crore, despite expectations of a stronger opening, especially with Yash playing Ravana. Meanwhile, the Telugu version collected Rs. 6 crore, followed by Tamil with Rs. 2.60 crore and Malayalam with Rs. 1.50 crore net on its opening day.
